newsitem.title: USA: Alzheimer's caseload could explode in midcentury.
newsitem.headline: Alzheimer's caseload could explode in midcentury.

text.p: The number of people with Alzheimer's disease could explode midway through the 21st century as the population ages, experts said on Wednesday.

National Association on Ageing (NIA) demographic expert Richard Suzman said there was a wide range of estimates of how many people would be older than 85 by 2050. But he said recent research tended to support the high end of estimates, or more than 30 million people.
Estimates also varied widely as to how many people older than 85 will suffer from Alzheimer's or other forms of dementia. Estimates vary from roughly 20 percent to 50 percent.

Experts agree that the population will age in the coming decades, but predictions of how many people will have Alzheimer's in 50 or 60 years are difficult, partly because no one can know whether treatments, preventatives or a cure will be available in coming years.

Suzman spoke at a briefing for science journalists in New York sponsored by the Alzheimer's Association and Bayer Ag, which is researching drugs. Association officials appealed for more research into the disorder, which robs people of their memories and thought processes and eventually kills them.
"Unless we substantially accelerate current programmes millions more Americans will be afflicted in coming years," said Edward Truschke, president of the association.
